title: Lewis and Clark expedition
why_famous: A landmark U.S. survey to the Pacific, made possible by Indigenous knowledge and guidance.
route_summary: Camp Dubois up the Missouri, across the Rockies and down the Columbia to Fort Clatsop; return along related routes.
source_title: National Park Service: Lewis and Clark trail maps
geometry_note: Principal outbound places only; the 1806 return diverged and is omitted rather than falsely folded into one line. River legs follow place anchors, not channel centerlines.

anchors.name: Camp Dubois
anchors.note: Expedition departure near the Missouri confluence.

anchors.name: Fort Mandan
anchors.note: 1804–05 winter camp; Mandan and Hidatsa homelands.

title: Xuanzang pilgrimage
why_famous: Collected Buddhist texts in India and brought them back to China, reshaping East Asian Buddhist scholarship.
route_summary: Chang'an via the Tarim oases and Central Asia to northern India, returning by the southern Tarim corridor.
source_title: British Library: Buddhist travellers and pilgrims
geometry_note: Only broad textual itinerary; city anchors are modern place approximations, and the passages between them are historical corridors, not a measured seventh-century track.

title: Ibn Battuta travels
why_famous: His Rihla records one of history's most extensive travel accounts across Afro-Eurasia.
route_summary: Selected documented stages: Tangier to Mecca, overland to Delhi, sea journey through the Maldives and Sumatra toward China, and later Sahara journey to Mali.
source_title: University of California Berkeley: The Travels of Ibn Battuta
geometry_note: Four selected journeys, with discontinuities and broad city corridors. China itinerary and chronology are debated; Quanzhou represents the reported port rather than a verified endpoint.

title: Marco Polo travels
why_famous: His account gave European readers a lasting picture of Yuan China and Asian trade routes.
route_summary: Venice to Acre, overland through Persia and the Pamirs to Yuan China; maritime return by Southeast Asia and the Indian Ocean.
source_title: Library of Congress: Travels of Marco Polo manuscript
geometry_note: Selected literary itinerary, not an independently verified track. Specific Silk Road legs and Chinese travel remain disputed; maritime return is kept separate.

title: Cherokee forced removal
why_famous: The U.S. government forced Cherokee communities from their homelands, causing widespread death and dispossession.
route_summary: A representative northern land route from southeastern Cherokee territory through Tennessee, Kentucky, Illinois, Missouri, and Arkansas to Indian Territory.
source_title: National Park Service: Trail of Tears route map
geometry_note: Represents one northern overland removal corridor, not all detachments. The NPS maps multiple land and water routes; place controls do not identify a single named detachment.

anchors.name: Red Clay council site
anchors.note: Cherokee homeland site near removal origin; not every detachment began here.

anchors.name: Golconda
anchors.note: Ohio River crossing region; precise route varies.

title: Oregon Trail migrations
why_famous: A major settler wagon corridor to the Pacific Northwest with profound effects on Native nations.
route_summary: Representative main corridor from Independence along the Platte through South Pass, the Snake and Columbia basins to Oregon City.
source_title: National Park Service: historic trail GIS
geometry_note: Collective migration over decades. This is a main-corridor place sequence; cutoffs and alternate river and wagon endings are omitted.

title: Gandhi's Salt March
why_famous: The 24-day march to the sea became a defining nonviolent protest against British colonial salt laws.
route_summary: Sabarmati Ashram through Gujarat villages to Dandi on the Arabian Sea.
source_title: Library of Congress: Salt March route planning
geometry_note: Named settlement sequence is indicative; individual village streets are not digitized from Gandhi's daily march log.

title: Burke and Wills expedition
why_famous: The celebrated Australian north–south crossing ended fatally on the return, despite assistance from Yandruwandha people.
route_summary: Melbourne to Menindee and Cooper Creek, north to the Gulf of Carpentaria mangroves, then back to Cooper Creek.
source_title: National Museum of Australia: Burke and Wills collection
geometry_note: Wills's historic map informs the northern stage. The Gulf anchor is a coastal mangrove region, not an ocean shoreline actually reached by the party.

anchors.name: Boulia region
anchors.note: Broad inland northward corridor control, not a documented camp.

anchors.name: Gulf mangroves near Flinders River
anchors.note: Northernmost mangrove region; no open sea sighting.

title: California Trail migrations
why_famous: A principal overland route of the Gold Rush and westward settler movement.
route_summary: Representative Humboldt River and Truckee River branch from the Missouri River through South Pass to Sacramento.
source_title: National Park Service: historic trail GIS
geometry_note: Selected Truckee branch of a network; bypasses and other Sierra crossings are excluded. Place-to-place segments are cartographic approximations.

title: Anza colonizing expedition
why_famous: A well-documented Spanish colonizing caravan reached the San Francisco Bay region from Sonora, accelerating the colonization of Alta California.
route_summary: Horcasitas to Tubac, Yuma, San Gabriel and Monterey; Anza then explored the San Francisco Bay with a smaller party.
source_title: National Park Service: Anza expedition campsite mapping
geometry_note: NPS distinguishes fixed from hypothesized camps; these are selected named controls, not the complete campsite GIS. Bay reconnaissance was by Anza's smaller party after the colonists stopped at Monterey.

anchors.name: Horcasitas
anchors.note: NPS fixed campsite; departure of mapped colonizing leg.

anchors.name: Gila–Colorado confluence
anchors.note: Yuma crossing with Quechan help; exact camp area varies.

anchors.name: Presidio of Monterey
anchors.note: Anza's smaller party departed after colonists settled.

title: Pony Express service route
why_famous: A celebrated relay mail service carried news between Missouri and California before the transcontinental telegraph.
route_summary: St. Joseph through Fort Kearny, Fort Laramie, Salt Lake City and Carson City to Sacramento.
source_title: National Park Service: Pony Express trail map
geometry_note: Service network represented by principal stations and crossings, not one rider's continuous trip. The Sacramento to San Francisco steamer continuation is omitted.

title: Mormon pioneer migration
why_famous: The 1846 evacuation and 1847 vanguard trek established a Latter-day Saint settlement in the Salt Lake Valley.
route_summary: Nauvoo across Iowa to Winter Quarters, then Brigham Young's 1847 vanguard by the Platte, South Pass and Fort Bridger to the Salt Lake Valley.
source_title: National Park Service: Mormon Pioneer Trail timeline
geometry_note: The 1846 Iowa evacuation and 1847 vanguard are distinct stages; anchors do not represent all later emigrant companies.

title: William Becknell's Santa Fe journey
why_famous: Opened a commercial route from Missouri to Santa Fe that became the Santa Fe Trail.
route_summary: Franklin, Missouri through the Arkansas River and Raton Pass corridor to Santa Fe.
source_title: National Park Service: Santa Fe Trail maps
geometry_note: Represents Becknell's first 1821 journey via the Mountain Route corridor; the later Cimarron Cutoff is intentionally not substituted. Exact 1821 track is not surveyed.

anchors.name: Fort Larned region
anchors.note: Arkansas River approach; fort built later.

anchors.name: Bent's Old Fort region
anchors.note: Upper Arkansas corridor; fort built later.

title: Coronado expedition
why_famous: A Spanish colonial expedition crossed the Southwest and Great Plains in a search for wealthy cities.
route_summary: Compostela region through Culiacán and the Southwest toward Hawikuh and the Rio Grande; later journey toward Quivira in the central plains.
source_title: National Park Service: Coronado route uncertainty
geometry_note: NPS states the entire route is unknown and Arizona evidence may redraw it. This schematic only joins broad regions; Hawikuh and Quivira identifications require caution.

anchors.name: Sonora corridor
anchors.note: Schematic desert control, not a documented camp.

anchors.name: Rio Grande pueblos
anchors.note: Tiguex province broadly located near Albuquerque.

anchors.name: Central Kansas region
anchors.note: Proposed Quivira region, not a fixed endpoint.

title: De Soto expedition
why_famous: A violent Spanish colonial incursion into southeastern Native homelands, followed by the first documented European encounter with the Mississippi River.
route_summary: Florida landing through the Southeast and across the Mississippi; the surviving party departed by river after de Soto's death.
source_title: National Park Service: de Soto expedition
geometry_note: The expedition alignment is contested. Region anchors are a schematic of scholarly proposals, not asserted town or village identifications.

anchors.name: Mississippi River near Memphis
anchors.note: One proposed river-crossing region; exact point unknown.

title: David Livingstone's African crossing
why_famous: His east–west and west–east journeys shaped European geographic knowledge while relying on African guides and networks.
route_summary: Linyanti to Luanda and back, then via Victoria Falls and the Zambezi basin to Quelimane.
source_title: Library of Congress: historical African expedition route map
geometry_note: A nineteenth-century comparative map supplies broad itinerary. Long rivers and overland legs are separated where identifiable, but exact crossings remain uncertain.

title: Heinrich Barth expedition
why_famous: Produced detailed geographic, linguistic, and cultural observations across North and West Africa.
route_summary: Tripoli through the Sahara to Lake Chad and west to Timbuktu, followed by return to North Africa.
source_title: Library of Congress: historic African expedition route map
geometry_note: Selected historically named oases and cities. The long Sahara passages are corridors on a comparative historic map, not surveyed travel positions.

title: John McDouall Stuart crossing
why_famous: A successful European south–north crossing of Australia and return, helping define the Overland Telegraph corridor.
route_summary: Adelaide via the interior to the north coast near present-day Darwin, then back along the same broad corridor.
source_title: National Museum of Australia: McDouall Stuart
geometry_note: Approximate chain of interior landmarks, not Stuart's measured camp log. Several places became named sites later and stand for nearby route regions.

anchors.name: Coober Pedy region
anchors.note: Desert corridor control; settlement founded later.

anchors.name: Alice Springs region
anchors.note: Central Australian corridor; town founded later.

title: Ludwig Leichhardt's first expedition
why_famous: An unusually long documented Australian traverse from the Darling Downs to Port Essington.
route_summary: Jimbour through Queensland and the Gulf country to Arnhem Land and Port Essington.
source_title: National Museum of Australia: Leichhardt expedition
geometry_note: This is the 1844–45 successful expedition, not Leichhardt's lost 1848 journey. Sparse regional controls do not reconstruct the historic daily route.

title: Gertrude Bell's Euphrates survey
why_famous: Her caravan survey documented archaeological sites along the Euphrates and informed later scholarship.
route_summary: Aleppo through the upper and middle Euphrates to Hit and Baghdad.
source_title: Library of Congress: Gertrude Bell caravan map
geometry_note: LOC's original map covers the east-bank Euphrates between Jerablus and Hit. The Aleppo approach and onward Baghdad link are less constrained; Mosul is excluded because it is not part of this specific mapped 1909 corridor.

anchors.name: Jerablus
anchors.note: Euphrates entry; LOC map begins here.

anchors.name: Hit
anchors.note: Middle Euphrates terminus of original map.

title: Aurel Stein's first Central Asian expedition
why_famous: A major archaeological survey of Silk Road sites, with cultural object removals now contested.
route_summary: Kashmir over the Karakoram to the Tarim Basin and Khotan region, returning to India.
source_title: British Museum: exploring the Silk Roads
geometry_note: Broad regional itinerary; pass selection and individual archaeological sites are not resolved by the summary source. Return route omitted.

anchors.name: Karakoram Pass
anchors.note: Representative mountain crossing; passage requires verification against the expedition diary.

title: Lady Anne Blunt's Arabian journeys
why_famous: Her published Arabian travels and surviving route map record two uncommon nineteenth-century European journeys through the region.
route_summary: Separate 1878 Beirut–Baghdad–Alexandretta and 1879 Beirut–Al Jawf–Hā'il–Baghdad–Būshehr itineraries.
source_title: Library of Congress: Lady Anne Blunt route map
geometry_note: Two itineraries are intentionally separate. The 1879 route via Al Jawf, Hā'il and Baghdad is corroborated by her account and contemporary descriptions; exact desert line and final Persian Gulf crossing remain indicative.

anchors.name: Alexandretta
anchors.note: Modern İskenderun; Mediterranean end of 1878 route.

anchors.name: Basra
anchors.note: Lower Mesopotamia corridor; precise onward transport uncertain.

title: Faxian pilgrimage
why_famous: His account of Buddhist sites and texts is among the earliest major Chinese records of travel to India.
route_summary: China via Central Asia to Buddhist sites in India; maritime return through Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia.
source_title: British Library: Buddhist travellers and pilgrims
geometry_note: Fourth/fifth-century itinerary is generalized to major regions; exact oasis sequence and Indian paths are not measured tracks. Return voyage is a separate segment.

title: Cabeza de Vaca traverse
why_famous: A survival account after the Narváez expedition shipwreck, involving years among Indigenous communities of the southern North American interior.
route_summary: Gulf shipwreck near Galveston Island followed by a disputed inland traverse toward northern Mexico and Culiacán.
source_title: Library of Congress: Cabeza de Vaca historical background
geometry_note: Proposed paths differ widely across Texas and northern Mexico. These few regional anchors are a corridor schematic, not a claim that each city was visited.

anchors.name: Galveston Island region
anchors.note: Approximate shipwreck and early captivity region.

anchors.name: South Texas interior
anchors.note: Broad regional control, not an identified campsite.

title: El Camino Real de Tierra Adentro
why_famous: A long-lived colonial road linking central Mexico to New Mexico, built over older Indigenous routes and tied to trade and colonization.
route_summary: Representative road corridor from Mexico City through Zacatecas, Chihuahua and El Paso to Santa Fe.
source_title: National Park Service: El Camino Real maps
geometry_note: This is a route network over centuries, not one person's trip. Historic alignments moved; place anchors define the corridor only.
